```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
using CEVE543Utils, Dates, DataFrames, Printf, Turing

here = dirname(@__FILE__)

miles_between(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2) =
    2 * 3958.8 * asin(sqrt(sind((lat2 - lat1) / 2)^2 + cosd(lat1) * cosd(lat2) * sind((lon2 - lon1) / 2)^2))

# NOAA Atlas 14 Texas 1-day annual maxima, read as in overview.qmd
function read_atlas14(path)
    rows = NamedTuple[]
    id, name, lat, lon = "", "", NaN, NaN
    for line in Iterators.drop(eachline(path), 1)
        isempty(strip(line)) && continue
        if occursin(r"^\d\d/\d\d/\d{4}", line)
            day, value = split(line)
            push!(rows, (; id, name, lat, lon, date=Date(day, dateformat"mm/dd/yyyy"), prcp_in=parse(Float64, value)))
        else
            fields = strip.(split(line, ","))
            id, lat, lon = fields[1], parse(Float64, fields[end-2]), parse(Float64, fields[end-1])
            name = join(fields[2:(end-4)], ",")
        end
    end
    return DataFrame(rows)
end

hobby_lat, hobby_lon = 29.6381, -95.2819
ams = read_atlas14(joinpath(here, "dur01d_ams_na14v11.txt"))
ams.year = year.(ams.date)
ams.miles = miles_between.(hobby_lat, hobby_lon, ams.lat, ams.lon)
near = ams[ams.miles .<= 25, :]
station_ids = unique(near.id)
n_stations = length(station_ids)
record_years = [count(==(s), near.id) for s in station_ids]
station_index = indexin(near.id, station_ids)

# No pooling: one maximum likelihood fit per station, as in overview.qmd
level_100yr_alone = [only(returnlevel(gevfit(near.prcp_in[near.id .== s]), 100)) for s in station_ids]
# Full pooling: one maximum likelihood fit to every station's maxima together
level_100yr_pooled = only(returnlevel(gevfit(near.prcp_in), 100))
# Full pooling of the shape only: station indicators give each station its own location and scale
indicators = [Float64.(station_index .== k) for k in 2:n_stations]
level_100yr_by_obs = returnlevel(gevfit(near.prcp_in; locationcov=indicators, logscalecov=indicators), 100)
level_100yr_shared_shape = [level_100yr_by_obs[findfirst(==(k), station_index)] for k in 1:n_stations]
```

## Motivation: nonstationary models

Nonstationary models do not fit the classical regionalization methods:

- a trend adds a coefficient at every station: $\mu_{s,t} = \alpha_s + \beta_s X_t$
- index flood and region of influence average stationary L-moments, which do not extend easily to covariates

How can we share information between similar locations in a **principled** way?

## Motivation: estimating nonstationary models

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Figure shown in class: Return levels at Little Sugar Creek from a stationary model (gray) and from nonstationary models (blue), with bootstrap 95% intervals; the nonstationary intervals are far wider, especially at long return periods [@serinaldi_undead:2015].
:::

## Case study: stations near Hobby Airport

- The `{julia} n_stations` NOAA Atlas 14 stations within 25 miles of Hobby Airport, from the overview.
- Data: 1-day annual maximum rainfall, `{julia} nrow(near)` station-years, with records of `{julia} minimum(record_years)` to `{julia} maximum(record_years)` years.
- Goal: a 100-year estimate at each station.
- Each pooling option below fits a different model to the same data.

## Four ways to pool

$$y_{s,t} \sim \mathrm{GEV}(\mu_{s,t}, \sigma_{s,t}, \xi_{s,t}), \quad \mu_{s,t} = \alpha_s + \beta_s X_t$$

- $y_{s,t}$: annual maximum at station $s$ in year $t$; $X_t$: a covariate.
- For each parameter, choose how much the stations share (today's fits are stationary, $\beta_s = 0$):

1. No pooling: fit every station alone.
1. Full pooling of every parameter: one distribution for all.
1. Full pooling of some: share some, often the shape.
1. Partial pooling of some: draw station values from a common distribution.

## No pooling

$$y_{s,t} \sim \mathrm{GEV}(\mu_{s,t}, \sigma_{s,t}, \xi_{s,t})$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

- Every parameter is fit at each station from its own record.
- One model, run once per station.
- Maximum likelihood fits give the `{julia} @sprintf("%.1f", minimum(level_100yr_alone))` to `{julia} @sprintf("%.1f", maximum(level_100yr_alone))` inch range of 100-year levels from the overview.

:::
::: {.column width="55%"}

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# y: one station's annual maxima
@model function no_pooling(y)
    μ ~ Normal(5, 5)
    σ ~ LogNormal(0, 2)
    ξ ~ Uniform(-0.5, 0.5)
    y .~ GeneralizedExtremeValue(μ, σ, ξ)
end
```

:::
::::

## Full pooling of every parameter

$$y_{s,t} \sim \mathrm{GEV}(\mu_t, \sigma_t, \xi_t)$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

- Every station has the same distribution.
- Same code as no pooling, fed every station's data.
- Longer records count for more.
- A maximum likelihood fit to all `{julia} nrow(near)` maxima gives a 100-year level of `{julia} @sprintf("%.1f", level_100yr_pooled)` inches at every station.

:::
::: {.column width="55%"}

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# y: every station's annual maxima, stacked
@model function full_pooling(y)
    μ ~ Normal(5, 5)
    σ ~ LogNormal(0, 2)
    ξ ~ Uniform(-0.5, 0.5)
    y .~ GeneralizedExtremeValue(μ, σ, ξ)
end
```

:::
::::

## Full pooling of some parameters

$$y_{s,t} \sim \mathrm{GEV}(\mu_{s,t}, \sigma_{s,t}, \xi_t)$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

- Like regional shape estimation.
- A maximum likelihood fit gives 100-year levels from `{julia} @sprintf("%.1f", minimum(level_100yr_shared_shape))` to `{julia} @sprintf("%.1f", maximum(level_100yr_shared_shape))` inches.

:::
::: {.column width="55%"}

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# station[i]: the station (1 to N) of y[i]
@model function shared_shape(y, station, N)
    μ ~ filldist(Normal(5, 5), N)
    σ ~ filldist(LogNormal(0, 2), N)
    ξ ~ Uniform(-0.5, 0.5)
    y ~ arraydist(GeneralizedExtremeValue.(
        μ[station], σ[station], ξ))
end
```

:::
::::

## Partial pooling of some parameters

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_{s,t} &\sim \mathrm{GEV}(\mu_{s,t}, \sigma_{s,t}, \xi_t), \quad \mu_{s,t} = \alpha_s + \beta_s X_t \\
\alpha_s &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(\bar\alpha, \omega_\alpha), \quad \beta_s \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\bar\beta, \omega_\beta)
\end{aligned}
$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

- $\bar\alpha$ and $\omega_\alpha$ are the mean and spread of the station intercepts; $\bar\beta$ and $\omega_\beta$ are the same for the trends.
- The shape is pooled fully: it is the hardest to estimate, and the region is small and flat.

:::
::: {.column width="55%"}

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# stationary: μ = α, so there is no β
@model function partial_pooling(y, station, N)
    ᾱ ~ Normal(5, 3)
    ω_α ~ LogNormal(0, 0.5)
    α ~ filldist(Normal(ᾱ, ω_α), N)
    σ ~ filldist(LogNormal(0, 2), N)
    ξ ~ Uniform(-0.5, 0.5)
    y ~ arraydist(GeneralizedExtremeValue.(
        α[station], σ[station], ξ))
end
```

:::
::::

## Hyperparameters

- The model estimates $\bar\alpha$, $\omega_\alpha$, $\bar\beta$, $\omega_\beta$ from the data, so the data decide how far each station is pulled toward the regional value.
- The stationary version on the last slide has $2N + 3$ parameters for $N$ stations: `{julia} 2n_stations + 3` for the `{julia} n_stations` stations near Hobby, and 500 draws took about 7 seconds on my laptop.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Ask

Whose $\alpha_s$ is pulled further toward $\bar\alpha$, a 30-year station or a 120-year one?
:::

## GEV parameters as a function of location

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_{s,t} &\sim \mathrm{GEV}(\mu_{s,t}, \sigma, \xi) \\
\mu_{s,t} &= \alpha + \beta_1 \mathrm{lat}_s + \beta_2 \mathrm{lon}_s
\end{aligned}
$$

- One model, fit to all stations at once.
- Week 6's covariate idea, with location in place of time.
- Five parameters, however many stations.
